messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai had always been drawn to the sea, and as a fisherman, he found solace in the rhythmic motion of the waves and the camaraderie of his crew. But it was on land, in a dingy room, that Kai's life took a drastic turn. He was captured by armed men while traveling abroad for work, subjected to days of brutal torture, and left with scars that went far beyond the physical. The memories of those dark days lingered, refusing to be extinguished. When Kai recalled the events, he felt an intense rage coursing through his veins, as if his body was reliving the trauma all over again. He would involuntarily assume the same defensive position, curled up and helpless, just like during the torture. The pain came flooding back too – a searing ache in his joints, a throbbing sensation in his head. It was as if no time had passed at all. As Kai navigated his daily life, he found himself becoming increasingly vigilant. He couldn't shake off the feeling of being watched or ambushed. Whenever he rode the bus to work, he'd sit near the driver, eyes scanning the other passengers for potential threats. Babies' cries, in particular, made him jumpy – their wails seemed to echo through his mind like a siren warning of impending danger. Kai couldn't explain why babies triggered this response; all he knew was that it made him want to flee or hide. His wife, Sophia, had given birth to their first child just a few months prior, and while Kai adored being a father, the constant crying and vulnerability of his infant son left him on edge. He began avoiding family gatherings, not wanting to be around when the baby got fussy. Feeling emotionally vulnerable was another trigger for Kai's anxiety. When Sophia tried to talk to him about their relationship or finances, he'd shut down, feeling overwhelmed by the prospect of opening up. "I just can't do this right now," he'd say, turning away from her and escaping into his own world. Kai started taking measures to feel safer in his environment. At home, he'd position himself with his back against a wall, scanning the room for potential escape routes or hiding spots. He'd listen intently for any unusual sounds – creaks, footsteps, whispers – convinced that someone might be lurking outside. His friends and family began noticing these quirks, but Kai couldn't explain them; all he knew was that it made him feel slightly more secure. One day, while working on his fishing boat, Kai spotted a coiled rope near the stern. In an instant, he envisioned using it as a makeshift noose or a whip – just like his captors had done. The sudden image sent a shiver down his spine, and for a moment, he forgot where he was. His crewmates noticed his distraction but said nothing. Sophia finally sat Kai down, her voice laced with concern, "You can't keep living like this, Kai. You're always on edge, always expecting something bad to happen. Our son needs a father who's present, not constantly looking over his shoulder." The words stung, and for the first time, Kai realized that he wasn't just fighting his own demons; he was also risking the well-being of those he loved. It was then that Kai knew he needed help – not just to cope with the memories but to reclaim his life from the shadows of torture. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, he whispered, "I don't want to be a prisoner of my own mind anymore."
